nameStory: The spider flower gets its spooky name from its six incredibly long, thin stamens that stick out from each bloom like spider legs! These thread-like stamens can stretch far beyond the petals, creating a delicate, leggy appearance that's unmistakable once you see it. Some folks also call it 'grandfather's whiskers' for the same wispy, elongated look.
description: Spider flower is a tall, dramatic annual that can tower up to 6 feet high in gardens and naturalized areas. This South American native has distinctive palm-shaped leaves with 5-7 narrow leaflets that spread like fingers from a central point. The real showstoppers are the clusters of pink, purple, or white flowers at the top of sturdy stems, each bloom bristling with those characteristic long, spindly stamens that give the plant its name. It blooms continuously from late spring through early fall, making it a garden favorite.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four-petaled flowers in pink, purple, or white with six extremely long, thin stamens that extend well beyond the petals like spider legs. The blooms have a light, citronella-like scent and cluster at the stem tops.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Palm-shaped compound leaves with 5-7 narrow, pointed leaflets radiating from a central point. Each leaflet can be up to 5 inches long with smooth edges, and the whole leaf sits on a long stalk up to 6 inches.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright annual growing 3-6 feet high with a sturdy central stem and spiral leaf arrangement. Plants spread 1-2 feet wide and have a distinctive architectural look in the landscape.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods up to 6 inches long that dangle below the flowers. These slender capsules split open when ripe to release small seeds, adding to the plant's spidery appearance.

habitat: In New England, spider flower is primarily found in cultivated gardens, but occasionally escapes to disturbed soils along roadsides or in vacant lots. It thrives in full sun and well-drained soils, tolerating both sandy and clay conditions. With only 71 observations recorded, it's not yet widely naturalized but may be spotted near residential areas where it's grown as an ornamental.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge from seed in late spring, developing their characteristic palm-shaped leaves first. Early growth is relatively compact before the dramatic height growth begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous flower production and rapid vertical growth. The plant reaches full height and the distinctive seed pods begin forming below spent flowers.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall until first frost. Mature seed pods split open and release seeds, while the plant begins to decline with cooler temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost, leaving only seeds in the soil. No above-ground parts persist through New England winters.

funFact: Spider flower's palm-shaped leaves are so similar to cannabis that it's frequently mistaken for marijuana by concerned neighbors and even law enforcement - leading to some awkward garden visits from authorities!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with cannabis due to its distinctive palm-shaped compound leaves and tall growth habit. The key difference is the flowers - spider flower produces showy clusters of spidery blooms with long stamens, while cannabis has small, inconspicuous flowers. Spider flower's citronella scent is also much different from cannabis.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'spider plant,' this species is completely unrelated to the common houseplant spider plant (Chlorophytum comosum) with the dangling plantlets. The shared name comes from their similarly 'leggy' appearance but they're in entirely different plant families.
compareHints: Spider flower is distinguished from its close relative spiny spider-flower (Cleome spinosa) by being generally taller and more robust in garden settings. Both share the characteristic long stamens and palm-shaped leaves, but garden spider flower tends to have showier, more colorful blooms and is the species most commonly cultivated in New England gardens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the more common Spider flower (Cleome houtteana) found in gardens, Spiny Spider-flower is distinguished by its stem spines and generally more robust, wilder appearance.
